nexusClaim.associationBasis: Authoring registers this relationship only as the population-level association the located alcohol-exposure literature supports. Alcohol consumption is a dose- and duration-dependent contributor to liver cirrhosis: a 2022 sex-specific systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 studies (2,112,476 women and 924,853 men; 4,301 and 4,231 cirrhosis cases) found a non-linear dose-response with substantially higher risk in women at every dose — 40 g/day pooled relative risk 9.35 (95 percent CI 7.64-11.45) in women and 2.82 (95 percent CI 2.53-3.14) in men, and 80 g/day 23.32 (95 percent CI 18.24-29.82) in women and 7.93 (95 percent CI 7.12-8.83) in men — with the female excess present for both morbidity and mortality (PMID 36926309); and a 2010 systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 cohort and case-control studies found indications of threshold effects, a significantly larger alcohol effect on cirrhosis mortality than on morbidity, and higher risk in women at the same average consumption (PMID 20636661). The preserved batch-91 anchor attaches to this registered relationship under ME-29: in a multicentre observational study of 115 heavy drinkers with alcoholic hepatitis versus 64 without, PTSD prevalence was 34 percent in both groups and PTSD was associated with higher average consumption (p=0.047) but NOT with heavy-drinking relapse or mortality (PMID 30080255), so the anchor is registered as exposure-population context — heavy-drinking populations in which alcoholic hepatitis arises — and not as a PTSD-to-liver claim. The registered claim is the narrowest these anchors jointly permit: the sustained heavy alcohol exposure that the alcohol-use-disorder diagnosis ordinarily marks is associated with a steeply dose- and duration-dependent elevation of population cirrhosis risk, higher in women at any given dose; no anchor establishes that alcohol use disorder caused any individual's cirrhosis.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation under 38 CFR 3.310 is established for any individual by these anchors: they quantify population dose-response between alcohol consumption and cirrhosis rather than individual etiology, and none separates alcohol's contribution from concurrent chronic viral hepatitis B or C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, hereditary hemochromatosis, autoimmune or cholestatic liver disease, or other hepatotoxic exposures — all of which the located literature treats as competing or coexisting causes that must be documented and excluded before attribution. The preserved alcoholic-hepatitis anchor measures PTSD in a population selected for heavy drinking and reports no association with heavy-drinking relapse or mortality, so it cannot carry an individual causal inference in either direction. The diagnosis-to-exposure mapping is disclosed on the face of the edge: the anchors quantify grams-per-day consumption and heavy-drinking populations rather than the diagnosis of alcohol use disorder as such, so the registered claim runs from the sustained heavy exposure the diagnosis ordinarily marks. Individual claims require a documented alcohol use disorder diagnosis with a quantified drinking history in grams per day, duration and pattern, objective liver-injury records with fibrosis staging, documented exclusion of viral, metabolic, autoimmune, cholestatic, hereditary and drug-induced competing etiologies, and qualified clinical opinion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesized cascade runs from sustained heavy alcohol consumption through hepatic ethanol metabolism — acetaldehyde adduct formation, oxidative stress, altered NADH/NAD+ redox balance, steatosis and de-novo lipogenesis, and progressive inflammation — to hepatocyte injury, fibrosis and, with continuing exposure, cirrhosis; the steep dose-dependence, the non-linear dose-response and the higher risk at a given dose in women are consistent with a toxic-metabolic exposure pathway, but no located anchor isolates that cascade in an individual rather than at population level, so the vector is stated as hypothesized rather than established. METABOLIC_OR_NUTRITIONAL is the closest available mechanism category and is used here as a toxic-metabolic-exposure label; it is not a claim about nutritional deficiency.
causalMechanism.secondaryVector: Where viral hepatitis B or C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, hemochromatosis or other chronic liver disease coexists, those processes independently drive fibrosis, and the located anchors do not separate their contribution from alcohol's in any individual.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on two dose-response systematic reviews and meta-analyses plus the preserved alcoholic-hepatitis exposure-population anchor, and deliberately not beyond them. At population level the located reviews quantify a non-linear dose-response with steep risk gradients (40 g/day: 9.35, 95 percent CI 7.64-11.45 in women and 2.82, 2.53-3.14 in men; 80 g/day: 23.32, 18.24-29.82 in women and 7.93, 7.12-8.83 in men; 24 studies, PMID 36926309) and threshold indications with a larger mortality than morbidity impact and higher risk in women at equal consumption (17 studies, PMID 20636661); the profile field registers that neither review, nor the alcoholic-hepatitis cohort (PTSD prevalence 34 percent with and without alcoholic hepatitis; PTSD associated with higher consumption, p=0.047, but not with relapse or mortality, PMID 30080255), establishes that alcohol use disorder caused any individual's cirrhosis, which is why the ASSOCIATION_ONLY classification carries NOT_ESTABLISHED etiological consensus rather than a WELL_ESTABLISHED claim. Individual claims require a documented alcohol use disorder diagnosis with a quantified drinking history, fibrosis-staged liver records, exclusion of viral, metabolic, autoimmune, cholestatic, hereditary and drug-induced competing etiologies, and qualified clinical opinion. The three anchors remain unverified pending qualified-human citation verification under docs/citation-verification-sop.md; this authored-corpus registration landed on 2026-10-04 under Stage 3a of the signed design together with its registry lockstep and the graph adjacency node.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Exposure-measurement and design limits: the dose-response anchors measure average grams of alcohol per day in observational cohort and case-control studies rather than the alcohol-use-disorder diagnosis itself, drinking is self-reported, and abstainer reference groups can include former drinkers who stopped because of illness, so measured exposure is subject to misclassification and sick-quitter bias; the dose-response is non-linear and the pooled estimates are sex-specific but not stratified by beverage type, drinking pattern or duration, so duration and pattern information must come from the individual record; the alcoholic-hepatitis cohort (115 with versus 64 without) is a heavy-drinking population selected for a multicentre observational study, its PTSD measure is a questionnaire screen rather than a diagnostic interview, and it reports no relapse or mortality association, so it supplies exposure-population context only; no located anchor separates alcohol's contribution from concurrent viral hepatitis B or C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, hemochromatosis, autoimmune or cholestatic disease, or other hepatotoxic exposures; and none reports cirrhosis incidence stratified by alcohol-use-disorder diagnosis, severity or treatment status.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Chronic viral hepatitis B or C, which the located literature treats as a leading competing cause of cirrhosis and which commonly coexists with heavy alcohol use

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, including diabetes- and obesity-driven disease, a rival and increasingly predominant cirrhosis etiology that can coexist with alcohol exposure
Hereditary hemochromatosis and other genetic or metabolic liver diseases, which produce cirrhosis independently of alcohol
Autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, which are immunologically driven chronic liver diseases
Drug-induced or other hepatotoxic exposures (for example methotrexate, amiodarone, isoniazid or acetaminophen toxicity), which injure the liver independently of alcohol
Alcohol exposure below the dose threshold the located reviews indicate, or a heavy-drinking pattern too brief to register in the population dose-response, which does not meet the claimed exposure
Non-hepatic contributors to the documented findings, including malnutrition, congestive hepatopathy and biliary obstruction, which must be evaluated before attribution

evidenceGaps: Diagnosis-versus-exposure mapping: the anchors quantify average grams of alcohol per day and heavy-drinking populations rather than a diagnosed alcohol use disorder, so an individual claim requires both the diagnosis and a quantified drinking history (dose, duration, pattern) rather than the label alone.

No located anchor separates alcohol's contribution from concurrent chronic viral hepatitis B or C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, hemochromatosis, autoimmune or cholestatic disease, or other hepatotoxic exposures, all of which must be documented and excluded before attribution.

Observational dose-response design: abstainer reference groups can include former drinkers who stopped because of illness (sick-quitter bias), drinking is self-reported, and the pooled estimates are not stratified by beverage type or drinking pattern, so the magnitude for any individual is approximate at best.

The dose-response is sex-specific with higher risk in women at any given dose, and the located reviews do not report cirrhosis risk stratified by alcohol-use-disorder severity, treatment status or abstinence duration at the individual level.

The preserved alcoholic-hepatitis anchor measures PTSD prevalence in a heavy-drinking population and reports no association with heavy-drinking relapse or mortality, so it supplies exposure-population context only and supports neither an individual alcohol-to-cirrhosis inference nor any PTSD-to-liver claim.
suggestions.rationale: Authoring registers the signed alcohol-use-disorder to chronic-liver-disease route (docs/catalog-identity-migration-design-2026-09-29.md) into the authored corpus under the design's Stage 3a, on the ordinary draft path because both mappings are drafts. The located evidence quantifies the population association between alcohol exposure and cirrhosis: a 2022 sex-specific systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 studies (2,112,476 women and 924,853 men; 4,301 and 4,231 cirrhosis cases) found a non-linear dose-response with substantially higher risk in women at every dose — 40 g/day pooled relative risk 9.35 (95 percent CI 7.64-11.45) in women and 2.82 (95 percent CI 2.53-3.14) in men, and 80 g/day 23.32 (95 percent CI 18.24-29.82) in women and 7.93 (95 percent CI 7.12-8.83) in men — present for both morbidity and mortality (PMID 36926309); and a 2010 systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 cohort and case-control studies found indications of threshold effects, a significantly larger alcohol effect on cirrhosis mortality than on morbidity, and higher risk in women at the same average consumption (PMID 20636661). The preserved batch-91 anchor PMID 30080255 attaches to this registered relationship under ME-29: in 115 heavy drinkers with alcoholic hepatitis versus 64 without, PTSD prevalence was 34 percent in both groups and PTSD was associated with higher average consumption (p=0.047) but NOT with heavy-drinking relapse or mortality, so the anchor is registered as exposure-population context — heavy-drinking populations in which alcoholic hepatitis arises — and not as a PTSD-to-liver claim; the direct ptsd to chronic-liver-disease edge stays withheld, superseded by the two honest windows, and no PTSD-to-alcohol-to-liver chain claim is made on the face of this edge. The edge is deliberately ASSOCIATION_ONLY: no located anchor establishes that alcohol use disorder caused any individual's cirrhosis, all three anchors are observational, none separates alcohol's contribution from viral hepatitis B or C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, hemochromatosis, autoimmune or cholestatic disease or other hepatotoxic exposures, and the anchors measure grams-per-day consumption rather than the diagnosis, so the registered claim runs from the sustained heavy exposure the diagnosis ordinarily marks. Boundaries carried on the face of the edge: the diagnosis-to-exposure mapping is disclosed; the alcoholic-hepatitis anchor's population is a severity-spectrum population selected for heavy drinking and is not evidence about PTSD outcomes; dose and duration govern the magnitude, with women at higher risk at any given dose; and alcohol use disorder is the alcohol-specific diagnosis while substance-use-disorder remains the broad discovery grouping, so this edge must not be read as evidence for non-alcohol substances. Window discipline: this is the only registered window from alcohol-use-disorder; a future liver-first window (for example cirrhosis-of-the-liver to alcohol-use-disorder) or a second alcohol-to-liver path would require npm run audit:crg redundancy adjudication before authoring, and the CRG note that ptsd to substance-use-disorder is already registered means a future ptsd to alcohol-use-disorder window will need parallel-targeting review at its own landing. The route's anchors (PMID 30080255, PMID 36926309, PMID 20636661) were confirmed absent from the registry and cleared by source-status preflight with zero blocking flags on 2026-10-04; they enter verified:false pending qualified-human citation verification under docs/citation-verification-sop.md, and the relationship row, the three source entities and the graph adjacency node were registered in lockstep with this suggestion on 2026-10-04.

Posttraumatic Stress Disorder in Patients with Heavy Alcohol Consumption and Alcoholic Hepatitis. Alcohol Clin Exp Res. 2018 Oct;42(10):1933-1938. doi:10.1111/acer.13862. PMID 30080255.
sourceReferences.note: Preserved batch-91 anchor, attached at authoring under ME-29 and registered as this edge's EXPOSURE-POPULATION anchor: a multicentre observational study screening heavy drinkers with alcoholic hepatitis (n=115) versus without (n=64) found PTSD prevalence 34 percent in both groups, PTSD associated with higher average alcohol consumption (p=0.047 on both tests) but NOT with heavy-drinking relapse or mortality, and PTSD in the alcoholic-hepatitis group not associated with higher relapse or mortality. The study measures PTSD in a heavy-drinking, alcoholic-hepatitis-selected population rather than the alcohol-use-disorder diagnosis or a dose-response, so it is registered as context for the exposure population in which alcoholic hepatitis arises, under the design's ME-29 discipline (preserved unregistered when the direct ptsd to chronic-liver-disease chain was withheld, attached to a registered relationship only at authoring). LIMITATIONS CARRIED: questionnaire screen rather than diagnostic interview, heavy-drinking selection, and no alcohol-use-disorder diagnosis or dose quantification of its own. Mapping approval is not citation verification; this source enters verified:false pending qualified-human citation review.

sourceReferences.citation: Llamosas-Falcón L, Probst C, Buckley C, Jiang H, Lasserre AM, Puka K, Tran A, Rehm J. Sex-specific association between alcohol consumption and liver cirrhosis: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Gastroenterol (Lausanne). 2022;1:1005729. doi:10.3389/fgstr.2022.1005729. PMID 36926309.
sourceReferences.note: Sex-specific dose-response anchor: systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 longitudinal and case-control studies (2,112,476 women and 924,853 men; 4,301 and 4,231 cirrhosis cases) modeling a non-linear dose-response by sex, registered as this edge's PRIMARY magnitude anchor because it supplies the sex-specific dose-response the edge's disclosures rest on: 40 g/day pooled relative risk 9.35 (95 percent CI 7.64-11.45) in women versus 2.82 (95 percent CI 2.53-3.14) in men, and 80 g/day 23.32 (95 percent CI 18.24-29.82) in women versus 7.93 (95 percent CI 7.12-8.83) in men, with the female excess present for both morbidity and mortality (PROSPERO CRD42022299680). LIMITATIONS CARRIED: pooled observational designs, self-reported and heterogeneous drinking measurement, reference categories that can include former drinkers, and no individual-level etiology or onset chronology. Mapping approval is not citation verification; this source enters verified:false pending qualified-human citation review.
